extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of The Spectator; early-18th-century literate English public; essayists and translators
extracted.subtask_description: Reflections and practical guidance for composing short periodical essays and translations (mottos, quotations, audience-accessibility, poetic style). Useful to essayists, translators, and editors producing material for a general literate public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of motto/quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a short, striking line (preferably from the poets) as a motto for a paper; it gives a finer turn to a thought and supplies a memorable opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Addison states: take the motto out of the Poets rather than prose because 'the former generally give a finer Turn to a Thought, and by couching it in few Words, and in harmonious Numbers, make it more portable to the Memory.' Use it to support paradoxical points and to show you are backed by good authorities; but remember many readers won't relish an obscure motto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accessibility for unlearned readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the body of the paper contains plain, intelligible material for readers who do not understand the motto or learned quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The motto is described as 'a Word to the Wise' and 'of little Use to an unlearned Reader'; therefore 'I take care to make Provision for them in the Body of my Paper.' In practice, include clear exposition and entertainment that does not rely on knowing classical references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include at least one memorable line in each paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to furnish every paper with at least one excellent line or image that will stick in the reader's imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author promises 'My Reader is therefore sure to meet with at least one good Line in every Paper' — use a striking phrase or simile to give the paper a portable, memorable moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use learned quotations to signal authority and attract certain audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations in Latin and other learned references can attract and edify particular audiences and signal erudition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: a preacher quoting Latin drew larger congregations; another copied standard Latin phrases to compete. Use learned quotations deliberately to appeal to readers who value scholarship, but balance with accessible content for broader readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful translation preserving imagery and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: A good translation should preserve every image and sentiment of the original while retaining the ease and spirit of an original in the target language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On translating Sappho: 'the Translation has preserved every Image and Sentiment of Sappho, notwithstanding it has all the Ease and Spirit of an Original.' Translator should avoid weakening the beauties of the original; this is difficult and requires careful fidelity to imagery and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing unnatural witticisms or forced conceits in lyric poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyric poetry should follow nature and simplicity rather than be overloaded with small conceits, turns of wit, or affected ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sappho is praised because she 'followed Nature in all her Thoughts, without descending to those little Points, Conceits, and Turns of Wit with which many of our modern Lyricks are so miserably infected.' Favor 'pathetick Simplicity' over artifice when translating or composing lyrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentation about the creative process (speed of composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not boast about how quickly a piece was produced or signal that speed is a badge of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticized example: a modern writer who 'had each Piece minuted with the exact Number of Hours or Days it cost him in the Composition' — this ostentation is seen as tasteless and inferior to genuine, well-considered labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject mechanistic/contrived methods for producing poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical processes or gimmicks for producing verse (tables, devices, machines, or charms) are to be regarded as spurious and unworthy of true poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several satiric examples are given: 'poetical logarithms' that produce Latin verses by table, a poet who composed on glass with a diamond, and the idea of a 'Mill to make Verses.' These are presented as absurd shortcuts and anti-patterns; genuine art requires real invention and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cryptic signatures/marks to intrigue readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscure letters or marks appended to papers can serve as playful mysteries that intrigue readers and create conversational interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author defends using letters like C, L, X (and possibly Q, Z, Abracadabra) as 'Cabalistical' marks or 'little Amulets or Charms to preserve the Paper against the Fascination and Malice of evil Eyes.' While whimsical, such devices may amuse or puzzle the public and are used intentionally to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and cater to audience preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of particular tastes within the readership and adapt small elements (like language of quotations) to please them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the author notes that 'the Ladies... declare themselves in a more particular manner pleased with my Greek Mottos.' Tailor small stylistic choices to the preferences of valued audience segments while maintaining overall accessibility.
